chapter: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
title: The Four Rhythm Aces vocal quartet
summary: In Kansas City he led a vocal quartet with Worthy Smith and Roy Johnson (whose sister Countess played with Andy Kirk), singing bass and playing uke.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: But drinking, I always liked straight bourbon whiskey. And I would just drink so much. But when I got with Floyd Hunter's band, they drank so much and got so drunk, til I said I didn't know what I was going to do. I was playing drums, so the bass player left, see. And so, when the bass player left, they couldn't get a bass player. Well, I'd been messing with the bass in Kansas City, anyway, just picking it up --
What, somebody would put their bass down and you'd pick it up?
Yeah, well, I had a quartet in Kansas City.
Oh, you did?
Yeah, it was called the Four Rhythm Aces.
Oh? Who did you have?
And we were singing. It was Worthy Smith, Roy Johnson, myself and -- what's that little fellow's name? He just died not too long ago.
Never mind, it'll come back to you.
I'll tell you who he was.
Yeah, yeah, you'll remember.
Well, anyway --
Well, did they have instruments or were you just singing? Somebody had to play the guitar?
I played the ukelele, you know, one of those things.
You could?
And we had a little tenor guitar, four-string, and tuned like a uke.
Oh, no kidding.
And, Roy, he played the guitar.
Yeah.
And he could chord on piano. And, see, his sister was Countess Johnson, played with Andy Kirk.
Oh, really?
Yes.
Oh, they say she was a very good piano player.
Very good.
Jay McShann was talking about her.
Oh, yes, she was a very good player.
He said she would (unintelligible), but she was a very good piano player.
That's right, she was. She's the one that took Mary Lou's place.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, Roy knew chords and things like that.
I see, yeah.
And so I sang the bass. I was the bass.
Oh, you did? No kidding?
And we had this group.
And you all sang.
And we all sang.
Yeah.
And played with it.
Yeah, accompanied yourself.
And then we'd do a little number where I would chord call it on the piano and little things like that.
Yeah, yeah. So you knew where those chords lay and all that.
Oh, yes, yes, see.
Did you know keys by then?
Yes, oh, sure, sure. Well, I learned that in school, the different keys, in high school.
Oh, just from the singing?
Yeah. Oh, sure, like I said, you had to sing your notes, else the music teacher wouldn't let you play your instrument.
So when you would hear something, would you be able to guess which key it was in?
Oh, sure, yeah, sure.
You were lucky, then, weren't you, to have got to that schooling. A lot of drummers don't get that at all.
No, that's right.
That was very good.
